steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper evaluating webcam-based eye-tracking (gaze) data as an alternative to human-annotated rationales for evaluating explainability (XAI) methods in NLP. Include a short contributions subsection and a preview of the results.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- reliable, trustworthy NLP applications: need to explain and interpret model decisions
- XAI evaluation often relies on human-annotated rationales; expensive; biased towards annotation guidelines or annotators' demographic
- lab-recorded gaze at least as expensive, but more intuitive: annotators solve task while reading; no post-processing annotations
- recording gaze during annotation suggested before; computer vision: gaze in models for attribute prediction promising
- webcam-based eye-tracking: standard webcam; much more cost-effective; catching up in data quality

2. This paper
- whether / to what extent webcam eye-tracking is a valid alternative to human rationales for evaluating XAI methods in NLP
- part one: eye-tracking dataset itself — data quality across languages, indicators of task difficulty, decoding gold-label rationales from the eye-tracking signal
- part two: attention-based explanations, Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), Gradient \,\times\, Input
- question answering (QA) in English, Spanish, German; 4 multilingual Transformer models

## Contributions.

3. Contributions
- first analysis of webcam-based eye-tracking as alternative to human-annotated rationales on text
- (i) gaze-based indicators for task difficulty; (ii) factors influencing data quality
- (iii) fine-tune mBERT, distilMBert, XLMR, XLMR-L on QA in English, Spanish, German; (iv) evaluate explanations against human rationales and gaze

4. Earlier work
- build on eye-tracking data + analysis of earlier study: entropy, decoding accuracy of fixation patterns
- XAI-based analysis: gaze as alternative to rationales for evaluating model explanations

5. Results preview
- Section 3: gaze gives additional linguistic information, could infer task difficulty
- decoding accuracy varies across languages; promising, especially German
- Section 4: gaze ranks explainability methods similarly to human rationales
- code: github.com/stephaniebrandl/rationales-eyetracking-xai

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To build NLP applications that are reliable and trustworthy, it is important to be able to explain and interpret the decision of a model. These Explainable AI (XAI) approaches are often evaluated with human-annotated rationales. Rationales are usually expensive and they are biased towards the annotation guidelines or the demographic of the annotators. Collecting human gaze data in a lab is at least as expensive as collecting rationales, but the annotation process is more intuitive, because annotators can just solve the task naturally while they read the text, and there is no need for extra post-processing annotations after the task is done. Recording human gaze during annotation tasks has been suggested before, and studies in computer vision have shown promising results when gaze is included in models for attribute prediction. Webcam-based eye-tracking recordings, where the data is collected with a standard webcam, are much more cost-effective, and their data quality is catching up.

In this paper we analyse if and how far webcam-based eye-tracking can be a valid alternative to human rationales for evaluating XAI methods in NLP. In the first part of the paper we focus on the eye-tracking dataset itself. We analyse the data quality across languages, look for indicators of task difficulty, and evaluate how far gold-label rationales can be decoded directly from the eye-tracking signal. In the second part we extend the analysis to attention-based explanations and also to Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and Gradient \,\times\, Input. We do this analysis for question answering (QA) in English, Spanish and German, and for 4 multilingual Transformer models.

## Contributions.

3. Contributions
- first analysis of webcam-based eye-tracking as alternative to human-annotated rationales on text
- (i) gaze-based indicators for task difficulty; (ii) factors influencing data quality
- (iii) fine-tune mBERT, distilMBert, XLMR, XLMR-L on QA in English, Spanish, German; (iv) evaluate explanations against human rationales and gaze

4. Earlier work
- build on eye-tracking data + analysis of earlier study: entropy, decoding accuracy of fixation patterns
- XAI-based analysis: gaze as alternative to rationales for evaluating model explanations

5. Results preview
- Section 3: gaze gives additional linguistic information, could infer task difficulty
- decoding accuracy varies across languages; promising, especially German
- Section 4: gaze ranks explainability methods similarly to human rationales
- code: github.com/stephaniebrandl/rationales-eyetracking-xai

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To build NLP applications that are reliable and trustworthy, it is important to be able to explain and interpret the decision of a model. These Explainable AI (XAI) approaches are often evaluated with human-annotated rationales. Rationales are usually expensive and they are biased towards the annotation guidelines or the demographic of the annotators. Collecting human gaze data in a lab is at least as expensive as collecting rationales, but the annotation process is more intuitive, because annotators can just solve the task naturally while they read the text, and there is no need for extra post-processing annotations after the task is done. Recording human gaze during annotation tasks has been suggested before, and studies in computer vision have shown promising results when gaze is included in models for attribute prediction. Webcam-based eye-tracking recordings, where the data is collected with a standard webcam, are much more cost-effective, and their data quality is catching up.

In this paper we analyse if and how far webcam-based eye-tracking can be a valid alternative to human rationales for evaluating XAI methods in NLP. In the first part of the paper we focus on the eye-tracking dataset itself. We analyse the data quality across languages, look for indicators of task difficulty, and evaluate how far gold-label rationales can be decoded directly from the eye-tracking signal. In the second part we extend the analysis to attention-based explanations and also to Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and Gradient \,\times\, Input. We do this analysis for question answering (QA) in English, Spanish and German, and for 4 multilingual Transformer models.

## Contributions.

This work is the first analysis of webcam-based eye-tracking as an alternative to human-annotated rationales on text. We look into (i) gaze-based indicators that could show task difficulty and (ii) factors that affect data quality in webcam-based eye-tracking. We also (iii) fine-tune 4 multilingual Transformer models (mBERT, distilMBert, XLMR, and XLMR-L) on question answering in English, Spanish and German so that we can (iv) evaluate model explanations against both human rationales and gaze.

We use the eye-tracking data and analysis of an earlier study and build on it by computing entropy and decoding accuracy scores of the fixation patterns that were collected. We also do an XAI-based analysis to look at gaze data as a possible alternative to human rationales for evaluating model explanations.

The results in Section 3 show that gaze gives useful additional linguistic information that could possibly be used to infer task difficulty. Decoding accuracy from gaze data is different across languages, and the results are promising, especially for German. Gaze data also ranks the explainability methods similarly to human rationales, so it could be an alternative for evaluating XAI methods, as we show in Section 4. Our code is available at: github.com/stephaniebrandl/rationales-eyetracking-xai.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In order to build reliable and trustworthy NLP applications, it is crucial to be able to explain and interpret a model’s decision. Such Explainable AI (XAI) approaches often rely on human-annotated rationales for evaluation [1]. These are usually expensive and biased towards annotation guidelines [2,3] or the annotators’ demographic [4]. Collecting lab-recorded human gaze data is at least as expensive as collecting rationales, but it offers a more intuitive annotation process, since annotators can naturally solve the task while reading the text, which eliminates the need for additional post-processing annotations once the task is completed. Recording human gaze during annotation tasks has been suggested in the past [5,6], and studies in computer vision have shown promising results when including gaze into models for attribute prediction [7]. Webcam-based eye-tracking recordings, where data is collected via a standard webcam, are on the other hand much more cost-effective and are catching up in data quality [8].

In this paper, we analyse whether and to what extent webcam-based eye-tracking can be a valid alternative to human rationales when evaluating XAI methods in NLP. In the first part of the paper, we focus on the eye-tracking dataset itself: we analyse data quality across languages, look for indicators of task difficulty, and evaluate to what extent gold-label rationales can be decoded directly from the eye-tracking signal. In the second part, we extend our analysis to attention-based explanations as well as Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) [9] and Gradient \,\times\, Input [10,11]. We perform this analysis for question answering (QA) in English, Spanish, and German, and for 4 multilingual Transformer models.

## Contributions.

This work is the first analysis of webcam-based eye-tracking as an alternative for human-annotated rationales on text. We investigate (i) possible gaze-based indicators of task difficulty and (ii) factors that influence data quality in webcam-based eye-tracking. Furthermore, we (iii) fine-tune 4 multilingual Transformer models (mBERT, distilMBert, XLMR, and XLMR-L) on question answering in English, Spanish, and German in order to (iv) evaluate model explanations with reference to both human rationales and gaze.

We build upon the eye-tracking data and analysis of [12], computing entropy and decoding accuracy scores of the collected fixation patterns. In addition, we perform an XAI-based analysis to investigate gaze data as a possible alternative to human rationales for the evaluation of model explanations.

The results in Section 3 show that gaze provides valuable additional linguistic information that could potentially be used to infer task difficulty. Decoding accuracy based on gaze data varies across languages, with promising results especially for German. As shown in Section 4, gaze data also yields a ranking of explainability methods similar to that of human rationales, making it a potential alternative for evaluating XAI methods. Our code is available at: github.com/stephaniebrandl/rationales-eyetracking-xai.
